chapter_theme: Fearlessness before an assembly is rarer than courage in battle, and it's the test of learning: knowledge that can't be spoken there is a sword in a frightened hand, and its holder counts for less than the unlearned and little more than the dead.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the distinction of those without fear of the assembly (721-723), one benefit (724), its cause, the study of logic (725), and the low standing of those who fear it (726-730).

721.reading: Those whose purity lies in knowing the body of words, having known the kinds, don't let their speech slip before the capable.
721.nuance: The second line is identical to 711's. There the same people adjust to their hearers, and here they keep from faltering. Parimelazhagar brings in fear from the chapter's title; the verse only says வாய்சோரார்.

positions.position: வகை is the kinds of assembly, and வல்லவை is a capable assembly. He records a reading as 'what they have mastered'.
positions.quote: கற்றுவல்ல அவை, அல்லா அவை என்னும் அவை வகையினை அறிந்து

positions.position: வகை is the kinds of harm that come from a slip.

722.reading: Those who make what they've learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned.
722.nuance: The verse is about reputation (எனப்படுவர்). Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that the world only knows the learned through such occasions, so public recognition depends on this one skill, not on how much is known.

723.reading: Those who die amid enemies are easy to find; those who don't fear within an assembly are hard to find.
723.nuance: பகையகத்து and அவையகத்து are parallel: the assembly is a battlefield with a higher casualty of nerve. This is one of the Kural's boldest reversals of martial values. Parimelazhagar reads எளியர் simply as 'many' and அரியர் as 'few', so the claim concerns numbers and isn't a ranking of worth.

724.reading: Make what you have learned go home before the learned, and take the more from those who know more.
724.nuance: Fearlessness has an epistemic pay-off. Parimelazhagar's reason: no one can learn everything, so speaking in a mixed assembly prompts others to speak. Manakkudavar goes so far as to define fearlessness of the assembly as this exchange.

725.reading: Learn by the proper path and with its measure, so as to give replies in the assembly without fear.
725.nuance: Fear is treated as a gap in training, not of temperament. The verse's ஆற்றின் அளவு is brief; Parimelazhagar expands it into grammar followed by logic, listing Nyaya terms for disputation. Pope follows him. That learned apparatus isn't in the verse itself.

726.reading: What is a sword to those who are not hard-eyed? What are treatises to those who fear a subtle assembly?
726.nuance: வன்கண் is once again positive, as in 632 and 689. Parimelazhagar's conclusion is that such people have no claim on the treatises, and this goes further than saying they fail to use them.

727.reading: The treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி in the midst of enemies.
727.nuance: The image relies on a period contempt, and Manakkudavar again drops the word, saying only 'one who fears'. Parimelazhagar works the comparison out carefully: field and sword are both good, so the failure lies wholly in the holder, as with the assembly and the book.

728.reading: Though they learn many things, they are of no use if they can't speak well and tellingly in a good assembly.
728.nuance: Parimelazhagar reads பயமிலர் as of no use to the world, and records another view, that they have no fruit from their learning. Who is deprived is therefore not settled, the world or the scholar. The verse's own 'good assembly' is the same condition as 719.

729.reading: They say that those who have studied and understood, and yet fear an assembly of the good, are lower than the unlearned.
729.nuance: என்ப, 'they say', reports this as public opinion. Parimelazhagar makes it pointed: such people benefit neither themselves nor others and have obtained only the pain of study.

730.reading: Those who, fearing the arena, can't make what they've learned go home are like the absent, even though they exist.
730.nuance: The chapter ends with a social death: to Parimelazhagar they are like the dead since the world doesn't count them. களன் can be a battlefield as well, so the word may close the chapter on the same comparison as 723, though Parimelazhagar glosses it as those seated there.

links.note: 780 calls a death that brings tears to one's ruler's eyes worth begging for, in the chapter on martial pride. 723 calls those who die among enemies easy to find. The Kural holds both, and each chapter's supreme value is deflated by the other.

410 makes the unlearned like beasts beside the learned. 729 places a kind of learned person below the unlearned. Learning that seemed to separate humans from animals is here worth less than nothing if the learned can't speak.
650 uses the image of a scentless flower for those who can't expound their learning. 728 and 730 give the assembly as the place of the failure, and fear as its cause, adding a diagnosis to the image.

source_issues: 721: Manakkudavar's text starts with a stray line fragment of the verse, and his closing 'அமைச்சியல் முற்றிற்று' appears at this verse.
724: Parimelazhagar's text places the label விளக்கம் after a clause of its own explanation.
725: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
727: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (ஔÿபுள்ளிÿவாள், for ஒள்வாள்) and his lemma reads பகையத்து. Manakkudavar's text reads பசையிண்கண் for பகையின்கண்.
